title: Episode 296: Richard the Lionheart: The Third Crusade, the Siege of Acre, and the Captivity of Dürnstein

The daring, chivalric, and mythic life of King Richard I, Richard the Lionheart: the Plantagenet warrior-king who captured the imagination of medieval Europe during the Third Crusade. Crowned in 1189, Richard famously declared he would sell London if he could find a buyer to fund his holy crusade to recapture Jerusalem from Sultan Saladin. Conquering Cyprus, storming the fortified city of Acre, and defeating Saladin at the Battle of Arsuf, Richard forged a legendary duel of mutual chivalric respect with his Muslim adversary. Shipwrecked on his return and imprisoned in the Austrian fortress of Dürnstein by Duke Leopold, Richard was ransomed for thirty-five tons of silver, only to be struck down by a crossbow bolt at the siege of Châlus. Discover Coeur de Lion.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, our Kings and Queens of England series examines the ultimate romantic warrior-monarch of the Middle Ages: the king who spent barely six months of his ten-year reign in England, whose military genius on the sands of Palestine made him an immortal legend. Here is George with the extraordinary life of Richard the Lionheart.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE GOLDEN DUKE OF AQUITAINE: 1157 TO 1189
Born in September 1157 at Beaumont Palace in Oxford, Richard was the third son of Henry II and Eleanor of Aquitaine. Cultured, towering, with auburn-gold hair and regal poise, Richard was his mother's favorite child, inheriting her radiant southern temperament and love for troubadour poetry and courtly song. Invested as Duke of Aquitaine at age fourteen in Limoges, Richard grew to manhood fighting the rebellious barons of Poitou, mastering the art of medieval siege warfare and storming supposedly impregnable cliffside fortresses like Taillebourg. Fiercely protective of his southern duchy and resentful of his father's refusal to acknowledge him as sole heir to the Angevin Empire, Richard allied with King Philip II of France to defeat his ailing father in 1189. Crowned at Westminster in September 1189, Richard viewed the English crown primarily as a financial engine to bankroll his supreme obsession: taking the Cross to liberate the Holy City of Jerusalem.  His mother Eleanor of Aquitaine cultivated in young Richard an intense passion for the chivalric ideals of the troubadour court at Poitiers, teaching him to compose lyrical Occitan verse and play the lute alongside master poets like Bertran de Born. Richard's military apprenticeship in the rugged limestone ravines of Aquitaine was an extraordinary education in siegecraft: when the rebel lord of Taillebourg deemed his clifftop castle unassailable, Richard stormed the lower town in three days, captured the outer barbican, and compelled the garrison to surrender, earning a terrifying reputation for battlefield ruthlessness. His alliance with King Philip II of France against his own father Henry II was an agonizing family tragedy that haunted Richard's conscience, driving his desperate desire to seek spiritual redemption through the holy crusade to Jerusalem.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE SALE OF ENGLAND AND THE CONQUEST OF CYPRUS: 1189 TO 1191
When the catastrophic news reached Europe that Sultan Saladin had destroyed the Christian army at the Horns of Hattin and captured Jerusalem in 1187, Richard was the very first northern prince to take the Crusader's vow. Upon ascending the English throne, Richard stripped the royal coffers bare: he sold royal castles, sheriffdoms, crown lands, and church offices to the highest bidder, famously joking to his chancellor: 'I would sell London itself if I could find a wealthy enough buyer!' Sailing with a fleet of one hundred war galleys, Richard was diverted by a Mediterranean storm to Cyprus, where the despotic Byzantine ruler Isaac Komnenos imprisoned shipwrecked crusaders. Richard launched a furious amphibious assault, conquering the entire island in fifteen days. Promising Isaac he would not place him in iron chains, Richard kept his literal word by binding the captive emperor in silver and gold fetters, selling Cyprus to the Knights Templar to finance his holy campaign.  Richard's radical fire-sale of English royal assets upon his accession in 1189 was an astonishing gamble: he released the King of Scots from his feudal oath of homage for ten thousand silver marks, auctioned off royal crown manors, and sold the bishoprics of Durham and Ely to the highest clerical bidders, treating his English kingdom merely as an overseas bank account. His amphibious conquest of Cyprus in May 1191 was a strategic masterstroke that altered Mediterranean history: Cyprus served as an indispensable naval supply depot and agricultural breadbasket that sustained the Crusader States for the next four centuries. When Richard married Princess Berengaria of Navarre in the chapel of St. George at Limassol, crowning her Queen of England, it was the only English royal wedding ever celebrated on foreign soil during an active military campaign.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE SIEGE OF ACRE AND THE CARNAGE OF THE SANDS: JUNE 1191
Arriving at the besieged Muslim port of Acre in June 1191, Richard found the Christian crusader army decimated by scurvy and dysentery. Though stricken with a severe tropical fever known as 'arnaldia' that caused his hair and fingernails to fall out, Richard refused to rest: carried on a silk litter to the frontline trenches, he fired his crossbow at Muslim defenders through loopholes in his wicker mantlet. Richard's massive catapults battered the stone walls until Acre surrendered in July 1191. But when Saladin delayed in delivering Christian prisoners, true cross relics, and promised ransom money, Richard made the ruthless, terrifying decision that stained his crusading glory: on the plain of Ayyadieh outside Acre, Richard ordered nearly three thousand Muslim prisoners marched out in chains and systematically slaughtered with swords and spears before the horrified eyes of Saladin's cavalry outposts.  The mutual fascination between Richard the Lionheart and Sultan Saladin was one of the legendary chivalric dramas of world history: when Richard fell desperately ill with fever beneath the walls of Acre, Saladin sent his personal Arab physicians across enemy lines bearing fresh snow from Mount Hermon and Damascus peaches to cool the English king's burning brow. Yet Richard's cold-blooded execution of two thousand seven hundred Muslim prisoners on the plain of Ayyadieh shattered this romantic chivalric facade: determined to march on Jerusalem and unwilling to spare hundreds of Christian guards to watch hostile captives, Richard watched dispassionately from horseback as his knights butchered the unarmed men with swords and axes, an atrocity that hardened Islamic resistance across the Levant.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE BATTLE OF ARSUF AND THE MARCH TOWARD JERUSALEM: SEPTEMBER 1191
Marching south down the Palestinian coast toward Jaffa in late summer 1191, Richard demonstrated military generalship of peerless discipline: he kept his infantry on the exposed inland flank with heavy shields to protect the cavalry from constant horse-archer harrying, with his fleet sailing parallel to supply water and rations. On September 7, 1191, in the coastal forest of Arsuf, Saladin hurled twenty-five thousand Muslim warriors against the crusader line in a thunderous assault. Richard ordered his knights to hold their ground under a hailstorm of arrows until Saladin's cavalry was fully committed; then, sounding royal trumpets, Richard led a crushing, unified charge of heavy cavalry that cleaved through the Muslim center and shattered Saladin's legendary aura of invincibility, earning the admiring respect of the Sultan himself.  The march down the dusty coastal plain from Acre to Jaffa was an extraordinary test of iron discipline under horrific sensory assault: the crusader army marched twelve miles a day in suffocating heat, with Saladin's horse-archers circling constantly like hornets, releasing clouds of iron-tipped arrows that stuck so thickly into the crusaders' padded gambesons that chroniclers described the infantry as resembling walking pincushions. At Arsuf, Richard's tactical composure was supreme: despite furious pleas from the Grand Master of the Knights Hospitaller to unleash an immediate counter-charge, Richard forced his men to hold their ranks until the Muslim horsemen had exhausted their arrows and dismounted; only then did Richard unleash three thousand armored knights in a thunderous, earth-shaking shock charge that broke the Sultan's center and routed Saladin's elite guard.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE BITTER RETREAT AND THE TREATY OF JAFFA: 1192
Despite his tactical victories, Richard confronted the brutal strategic reality of Middle Eastern warfare: twice advancing to within twelve miles of Jerusalem, to Beit Nuba, Richard could see the distant towers of the Holy City gleaming in the sun. Weeping bitterly, Richard held his shield before his face, declaring that he who could not liberate the city of Christ was unworthy to behold it. Richard knew that capturing the city was militarily impossible: the crusaders lacked the manpower to garrison Jerusalem while maintaining water lines across scorching deserts. Learning that his treacherous younger brother Prince John was conspiring with Philip of France to usurp his English throne, Richard negotiated the Treaty of Jaffa with Saladin in September 1192: Jerusalem remained under Muslim control, but Christian pilgrims were granted unarmed, unmolested access to the Holy Sepulchre, and crusaders retained the coastal ports from Tyre to Jaffa.  The heart-wrenching decision to turn back from the threshold of Jerusalem at Beit Nuba in the freezing winter rains of 1192 was Richard's supreme moment of military realism over romantic zeal: his engineers pointed out that even if the crusaders breached the stone walls of the Holy City, Saladin would immediately sever the mountain water cisterns and encircle the Christian army, turning Jerusalem into a slaughterhouse for its conquerors. The three-year truce of Jaffa negotiated between Richard and Saladin's brother Al-Adil was a realistic diplomatic triumph: Christian pilgrims were granted safe, unarmed passage to pray at the Holy Sepulchre, and the coastal trading ports were secured. When Saladin sent fresh horses to Richard during a desperate skirmish outside Jaffa, observing that so noble a warrior should not fight on foot, it cemented an eternal mutual respect between the two greatest commanders of the medieval world.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE CAPTIVITY OF DÜRNSTEIN AND THE KING'S RANSOM: 1192 TO 1194
Sailing home disguised as a humble merchant named 'Brother Hugo', Richard was shipwrecked near Aquileia on the northern Adriatic coast. Attempting to cross German territory in secret, Richard was recognized in a tavern outside Vienna when a servant attempted to spend rare Syrian gold bezants. He was arrested by Duke Leopold of Austria—whom Richard had insulted at Acre by casting Leopold's ducal banner into the dirt—and locked in the remote cliffside castle of Dürnstein overlooking the Danube. Holy Roman Emperor Henry VI demanded an astronomical ransom of one hundred and fifty thousand silver marks—equivalent to two and a half times the annual revenue of the English crown. For fourteen months, England was stripped to the bone: every church surrendered its silver chalices and gold crosses, and a crushing twenty-five percent property tax was levied across the shires to pay the King's Ransom, securing Richard's release in February 1194.  The dramatic arrest of King Richard outside Vienna in December 1192 read like a medieval thriller: disguised in rough peasant wool and turning roasting capons on a kitchen spit in an inn at Erdberg, Richard was betrayed by his arrogant refusal to remove a magnificent ruby ring from his finger. Duke Leopold of Austria, still smarting from Richard's insult at Acre where the English king had trampled Leopold's ducal standard into the mud, handed Richard over to Emperor Henry VI. The romantic French legend of the minstrel Blondel traveling from castle to castle singing the king's favorite ballad until a voice answered from a high barred window in Dürnstein captured the imagination of Europe; but in reality, Richard's release was secured by thirty-five tons of raw silver bullion extorted from the churches and peasants of England.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE CROSSBOW OF CHÂLUS AND THE LION'S REST: 1199 AND LEGACY
Returning briefly to England in March 1194 to be re-crowned and forgive his groveling brother John, Richard spent the final five years of his life in France, building his magnificent limestone fortress Château Gaillard on the Seine to defend Normandy against Philip Augustus. In March 1199, while besieging the minor castle of Châlus-Chabrol in the Limousin over a rumored buried horde of Roman gold, Richard rode out without his shield, waving to a lone defender standing on the ramparts holding a frying pan as a makeshift shield. The man loosed a crossbow bolt: the iron bolt struck Richard in the shoulder, near the neck. When a clumsy surgeon hacked at his flesh to extract the iron arrowhead, gangrene set in. Summoning the youth who shot him, Richard pardoned the archer and ordered him given one hundred shillings, before dying in his mother Eleanor's weeping arms on April 6, 1199, at age forty-one. Richard the Lionheart's heart was buried at Rouen, his body at Fontevraud Abbey, leaving behind an immortal chivalric legend of unmatched bravery.  Richard's construction of Château Gaillard—the 'Saucy Castle' perched high above the chalk cliffs of Les Andelys on the Seine—was an engineering masterpiece of concentric fortification that Richard boasted he could defend even if its walls were made of butter. His sudden, tragic death at the insignificant siege of Châlus-Chabrol in April 1199 was a bizarre, inglorious end for Europe's greatest general: an iron crossbow bolt fired by a lone defender named Pierre Basile struck the king's unarmored shoulder. When gangrene spread through his flesh, Richard showed magnanimous Christian mercy on his deathbed, ordering the young crossbowman brought before him, pardoning him and bestowing a gift of silver. King Richard I was the quintessential warrior of European chivalry: a towering lion who lived for the thunder of battle, whose legend still echoes across the sands of Palestine and the stone halls of England.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
Thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories. Richard the Lionheart's crusading glory and dramatic death left the Angevin Empire in the hands of his younger brother. Join us next week as Rebecca returns with the disastrous reign of King John, the tragedy of the lost jewels in the Wash, and the signing of Magna Carta at Runnymede. Until then, stay curious.
